name: St. Johann im Walde
kurzbeschreibung: Tiny scattered village in the Drautal valley, surrounded by untouched mountain wilderness and traditional Osttirol way of life.
beschreibung:
St. Johann im Walde lies on a sun-exposed terrace high above the Osttiroler Drautal at 1,068 meters above sea level, within the district of Lienz. The village with around 300 inhabitants is one of the smallest municipalities in Osttirol and has preserved its village character – numerous farms are spread as a classic scattered village across the wide meadows and slopes around the Parish Church of St. John the Baptist.

The location at the foot of the Hochgrabe and with views of the Lienzer Dolomiten makes St. Johann im Walde a starting point for quiet hikes away from the main routes. The Panoramaweg toward Leisach or tours to the Bocksteinkapelle, a small pilgrimage site on a hill above the Drautal, show the untouched side of Osttirol. In winter, groomed cross-country ski trails lead across the open high plateau, and the nearby Schobergruppe remains an insider tip for ski tourers looking for quiet slopes.

The Osttiroler way of life is evident here in the many actively managed farms that sell regional products such as Osttiroler Schafskäse, Speck and Brot directly. Anyone not looking for a place to stop with a giant menu, but rather a cup of coffee with a farmer on the terrace, is in the right place here. St. Johann im Walde is not a place for big-city expectations – those who accept that get honest Osttiroler hospitality and scenery that does not yet feel staged. 🏘️
text:
Overview

St. Johann im Walde is located at an altitude of 748 meters in the sunny central Iseltal valley in East Tyrol’s Lienz district, positioned midway between the town of Lienz (14 km downstream) and Matrei in Osttirol (14 km upstream). Home to roughly 300 residents across an area of nearly 33 square kilometers, the municipality straddles the glacier-fed Isel river—the last free-flowing glacial river in the Alps. The territory stretches from the valley floor through high sunny hamlets like Oberleibnig (1,244 m) to the 3,000-meter peaks of the Schober Group within Hohe Tauern National Park. St. Johann im Walde represents a tranquil retreat of unspoiled nature, defined by authentic mountain farming traditions, roaring alpine torrents, and immediate access to cycling and hiking trails.

History

The settlement was first documented in 1177 as Capella s. Joannis in silva (chapel of Saint John in the forest) in a papal confirmation issued by Pope Alexander III for Innichen Abbey. The name reflects its patron saint John the Baptist and the dense alluvial woodlands that once covered the valley floor. For centuries, subsistence farming and forestry along the steep flanks of the Leibnitztal valley sustained the community. A transformative event occurred in September 1965, when catastrophic flooding of the Isel river ravaged the valley. During reconstruction, the parish church of Saint John the Baptist was expanded in modern style between 1968 and 1970 by architect Norbert Heltschl, preserving its 1503 late Gothic choir as a baptismal chapel. The high-altitude hamlet of Oberleibnig was connected only by mule tracks until a small passenger cable car was constructed.

Getting there

St. Johann im Walde enjoys excellent year-round access via the East Tyrolean road network. By car, federal highway B108 (Felbertauernstraße) runs directly through the valley: approaching from the north (Salzburg/Kitzbühel), pass through the Felbertauern Tunnel via Mittersill and Matrei, while drivers from Lienz reach the village in just 12 minutes north along the B108. Rail travelers arrive at Lienz railway station on the Drautal line. From Lienz, VVT regional bus line 950 operates hourly through St. Johann im Walde towards Matrei and Prägraten. Regional bus travel is complimentary for overnight visitors holding the Osttirol guest card.

Tips

Cyclists love the level Isel Valley Cycle Path (R12), winding along the banks of the glacial river between Lienz, St. Johann, and Matrei. Walkers can follow stages of the celebrated Iseltrail, tracing the river towards its glacial origins. For an alpine adventure, hike through the rugged Leibnitztal valley along the crashing Leibnizbach stream to the Leibnizalm pasture (1,908 m) and continue to the Hochschoberhütte (2,322 m), the main base for climbing Mount Hochschober (3,242 m). A unique regional attraction is riding the historic small-cabin cable car from the valley up to the sunny terrace of Oberleibnig (1,244 m) for sweeping views across the Lienz Dolomites.
